children.value: Modeling the term structure as a continuous function of maturity 🌊📈

children.label: Modeling the term structure as a continuous function of maturity 🌊📈

children.value: n Chapter Three, ordinary least squares (OLS) was used to estimate zero prices utilizing 302 bonds. These estimates spanned maturities ranging from a few days to almost ten years. In total, 193 discrete zero prices were estimated to cover a timeline of more than 3,600 actual days. ⏳ Moreover, we were only able to use 302 of the 399 bonds included in our dataset, resulting in sparse estimates at discrete dates and a truncated maturity profile. 📈⚠️

Many interpolation methods exist offering varying degrees of accuracy for filling these gaps. A common approximation applies a cubic spline between adjacent estimates. Although this results in a smooth, continuous curve, the purely mathematical process ignores the underlying structure of the data.

🔮 Consider an analogy: If you know a dataset is generated by a sine wave, you only need to estimate four parameters to perfectly map every point on the curve. A cubic spline, however, is heavily dependent on the number of observations; it requires calculating new polynomial coefficients for every single interval between data points. Because it ignores the underlying “shape” of the data, a spline cannot reliably extrapolate maturities beyond our truncated OLS estimates. 🛑🧮
Nelson and Siegel (1987) address the problem by focusing on four attributes of the term structure of interest rates:
The most basic question is the level of interest rates—whether rates are generally high or low. 📏
: The slope indicates if the rates are increasing or decreasing with maturity, a result that might reflect market expectations about inflation or monetary policy. 📐

: The shape indicates if there is a so-called “hump” in the term structure—a period when the pattern of rates and maturity deviates from the underlying slope via an increase or decrease in rates that is eventually reversed. 〰️🐫
: Determines how the slope and shape components are expressed over maturity dates, pacing how quickly their mathematical influence fades over time. ⏳⚖️

Because the Nelson-Siegel model relies on only these few parameters, it is highly parsimonious—allowing it to accurately capture complex, real-world term structures while avoiding the overfitting and extrapolation issues common in purely mathematical interpolation methods like cubic splines. We now introduce a widely used extension of this model incorporating additional parameters allowing for a second change in the shape (or a secondary hump) of the term structure.

The Nelson-Siegel model is remarkably flexible, but its single shape parameter limits it to modeling term structures with only one hump or dip. Sometimes the term structu8re exhibit more complex, “S-shaped” patterns, featuring both a hump and a trough at different maturities.〰️🔄 To accommodate this, Lars Svensson (1994) introduced a widely adopted extension. The Svensson model adds a second curvature term to the equation, bringing the total number of parameters to six:

By utilizing two distinct scaling parameters (

Nelson-Siegel vs. Svensson: Flexibility vs. Overfitting ⚖️💥

children.label: Nelson-Siegel vs. Svensson: Flexibility vs. Overfitting ⚖️💥

children.html: β3\beta_3β3​
τ2\tau_2τ2​

children.value: parameters in the Svensson extension provides immense flexibility, allowing the model to trace complex yield curve anomalies. The increased flexibility introduces a classic econometric problem: overfitting. ⚠️

A highly parsimonious model like the four-parameter Nelson-Siegel framework effectively filters out “noise”—such as the idiosyncratic mispricing of individual bonds or temporary liquidity premiums—and captures the true underlying shape of the term structure. 🛡️ Adding the Svensson parameters makes for a more sensitive model that, when applied to a sparse dataset, may twist and contort to fit the pricing errors of specific bonds. While the in-sample fit may improve, the model’s ability to extrapolate or price out-of-sample bonds reliably may degrade! 🛑📉
When to use the extended model? 🤔💼

children.label: When to use the extended model? 🤔💼

children.value: Choosing between the standard Nelson-Siegel model and the Svensson extension depends entirely on the complexity of the observed market and the density of the dataset.

Should be the default choice for standard market conditions. It is highly stable, robust to sparse data, and perfectly capable of mapping monotonic (upward, downward, or flat) and single-humped curves.

Should be reserved for specific market environments where the yield curve exhibits a clear, observable “S-shape” or double hump. Many central banks utilize the Svensson model to publish their official daily yield curves, but they rely on densely populated datasets of highly liquid bonds. For smaller datasets—such as our sample of 399 bonds—the extension is only justified when there is a clear secondary hump in the data. A characteristic that is not present in our dataset. ❌📊
